Lord’s Paradox

 In an article entitled A Paradox in the Interpretation of Group
 Comparisons (1967), Lord introduced a deceptively simple
 conundrum that defied attempts at resolution for nearly 15 years:

 A large university is interested in investigating the effects
 on the students of the diet provided in the university
 dining halls and any sex differences in these effects.
 Various types of data are gathered. In particular, the
 weight of each student at the time of his arrival in
 September and his weight the following June are
 recorded [Lord, 1967, p. 304].

Lord’s Paradox

 The paradox arises from two seeminly conflicting analyses of the
 data performed by two statisticians:
 Statistician 1 Performs a gain score analysis for the two sexes and
 shows zero average gain for both.
 Statistician 2 Performs an ANCOVA analysis and demonstrates a
 significant difference between the adjusted June
 weights of the two sexes.
 The paradox: One analysis indicates that the diet produces a
 differential effect for the two sexes while the other analysis
 suggests that it does not.

Lord’s Paradox Redux
 Lord (1973) extended the paradox to situations involving two groups
 and two treatments:

 . . . consider the problem of evaluating federally funded
 special education programs. A group of disadvantaged
 children are pretested in September, then enrolled in a
 special program, and finally posttested in June. A control
 group of children are similarly pretested and posttested but
 not enrolled in the special program. Since the most
 disadvantaged children are selected for the special
 program, the control group will typically have higher pretest
 scores than the disadvantaged group [Lord, 1973, p. 235].

Lord’s Paradox Solution

 An elegant solution to the paradox was provided by Holland
 and Rubin (1983) in a Festschrift devoted to Lord.
 The paradox lies with the incompatible causal inferences one
 wishes to draw from the data: differential effectiveness versus
 no-differential effectiveness.
 In both forms of Lord’s Paradox, a causal conclusion rests on
 an assumption concerning an unobservable control group.
 Holland and Rubin derive necessary conditions for the control
 group in order that the causal conclusions hold.
 Since the control group is unobservable, these conditions
 must be tested based upon knowledge of the given situation.

Rubin’s Causal Model

 Causality [Holland, 1986] with regard to effect t, relative to
 effect c, is conceived as the difference in outcome on unit u as
 measured by Y :

 Yt (u) − Yc (u)
 It is impossible to simultaneously observe and measure t and c
 applied to u.
 Scientists work around this difficulty by exploiting homogeneity
 and invariance assumptions with regard to the observational
 units.
 Statisticians, for example, consider average causal effect by
 utilizing random assignment of units:

 Effect = (Yt − Yc ) = (Yt ) − (Yc )

Using Teachers as the treatment

 The scenarios utilized within Lord’s paradox are not unlike current
 situations in which one wishes to determine the quality of a given
 teacher:
 Students, assigned to one of four teachers, are
 administered a pre-test at the beginning of the school
 year and a post-test at the end of the school year. Three
 statisticians, attempting to determine teacher efficacy,
 perform three types analyses: gain score analysis,
 ANCOVA, and mixed-effects analysis using using pre-test
 and post-test scores.

 To investigate this scenario, “toy" data is produced for the four
 teachers.

Rubin’s Causal Model

 Assuming one could assign students at random to both teachers
 and “control", the average causal effects associated with each
 teacher, T , is given by:

 ∆i = (Yt − Yc |T = i )
 To compare teachers i1 and i2 , one computes the difference of
 the average causal effects:

 ∆ = ∆ i1 − ∆ i2
 = (Yt |T = i1 ) − (Yc |T = i2 ) − (Yt |T = i1 ) − (Yc |T = i2 )
    

 = (Yt |T = i1 ) − (Yt |T = i2 ) − (Yc |T = i1 ) − (Yc |T = i2 )

Assumptions

 Estimating differential teacher effect requires one to make
 certain assumptions concerning what would happen to the
 same children under “control" conditions.
 The three statisticians make the following assumptions
 concerning their control groups:
 Statistician 1 The gain score analysis assumes the unobserved
 control group’s post-test score would equal their pre-test
 score, Yc = a. In some situations [Wainer, 1991] this is a
 justifiable assumption.
 Statistician 2 The ANCOVA analysis assumes the post-test
 score is a linear function of the pre-test score, Yc = a + bX .
 Statistician 3 The Mixed-effects analysis (random
 intercepts/fixed slopes) has analogous assumption to
 ANCOVA. The difference being the BLUPs of the residual
 effects.

Summary

 Different analyses can lead to irreconcilable conclusions
 regarding the efficacy of teachers.
 These differences arise from the causal claims made about
 the teachers under consideration.
 Following Rubin’s Causal Model, reconciling these differences
 requires one to make arguments concerning the behavior of
 unobservable control groups.
 Mixed-effects analyses, like gain score and ANCOVA
 analyses, have accompanying assumptions that must be
 fulfilled in order that causal claims hold.
